newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica's De Klerk denounces apartheid-era killers.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica's De Klerk denounces apartheid-era killers.

text.p: Former South African president F.W. de Klerk on Wednesday denied knowledge of a range of apartheid murders and denounced those responsible as cold- blooded killers.
De Klerk, under cross-examination by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, renewed his apology for apartheid but said he had committed no crime for which he required amnesty.
He told the commission he had been as shocked as anyone else by disclosures of murders, kidnappings and torture sessions by senior police officers in applications for amnesty.

But in one heated exchange with commission lawyer Glen Goosen, de Klerk refused to answer questions on a defence force document apparently condoning assassinations of black activists. He said he needed time to study the document and would reply later to written questions.
"During my presidency I went out of my way to get to the bottom of the truth and to find and prosecute the perpetrators of dastardly deeds," de Klerk said.
"I have never condoned gross violations of human rights and reject any insinuation that it was ever the policy of my party or my government."
De Klerk said maverick security policemen who objected to his steps to dismantle apartheid from 1990 were responsible for some of the atrocities that had been committed.

"The security people who had to guard me feared for my life, that I might have been assassinated by such elements. They were as much against the reforms as they were against the African National Congress (ANC)," de Klerk said.

Goosen asked him to respond to a series of notorious security force actions over the last three decades, including the activities of the "Vlakplaas" police hit squad and the recently discovered bodies of 12 assassinated ANC activists.
De Klerk said such actions were "absolutely unacceptable" and fell outside what a policeman or soldier could have interpreted government policy to have been.
Goosen said a police general and several colonels had applied for amnesty after confessing to having killed the 12.

"I was not in favour of changing the law to allow cold-blooded murderers to go free," de Klerk replied, referring to negotiations with the ANC that led up to South Africa's first all-race elections in 1994 and also provided for the kind of amnesties now being offered.
"Whoever did that, was not executing government policy."
Commission head Archbishop Desmond Tutu intervened to say the list of actions presented by Goosen extended over a long period and involved people of senior rank, including police commissioners.
"It becomes difficult to see how one can sustain a position that it was just a few bad eggs," Tutu said.
Goosen said the commission had heard evidence of 1,200 separate acts of torture by apartheid security forces and the practice appeared to have been systematic and routine.

On the Vlakplaas hit squad, whose commander Eugene de Kock has been sentenced to life imprisonment for a series of murders, de Klerk said four police generals had told him they were unaware of what de Kock was doing.
He repeated an earlier acknowledgment by the National Party that it accepted responsibility for having created "an atmosphere conducive to human rights violations" by police.
"They (the police) had to fight a revolutionary onslaught which had as its...goal to make South Africa look like Zaire is looking today...It was underground, it used terrorist methods.
"The result was more authority to security forces to fight the war, a very specific type of war," de Klerk said.
"Across the world where this type of war has occurred, there have been aberrations."

The truth commission was set up in 1995 to uncover as much as possible of the human rights abuses and crimes committed by all sides during apartheid. Earlier this week it questioned the ANC about its activities.
